1.title: Know the words of teaching a hobby
1.intro: A hobby course helps adults or children learn a skill for pleasure. Start with the words.
pts: Learn the terms: lesson plan, outcome, level, material, demo, practice, feedback, class size.
An outcome says what a learner can do at the end, such as 'knit a flat square'.
Beginners need small steps, plain words and quick wins.
Pick one hobby you know well and list five things a beginner must learn first.
1.ex: Outcome: 'By the end of class, you can cast on and knit ten rows.'
1.act: List five outcomes for a beginner class in your hobby, each starting with a verb.
1.std: Task: write five outcomes. Condition: for one beginner class. Standard: each starts with a verb that can be seen, such as make, draw, name or play.

2.title: Explain how a class is planned and run
2.intro: A good class has a shape. Learners should do more than listen.
pts: The shape: welcome, show, try, feedback, try again, wrap-up.
Plan time: ten minutes of showing and the rest for practice.
List materials and tools and who brings them.
Plan for slow and fast learners with an easy and a harder task.
2.ex: A 90-minute pottery-style class: 10 welcome, 15 demo, 45 practice, 10 feedback, 10 clean-up and next steps.
2.act: Write a 90-minute plan with times and a materials list.
2.std: Task: write a lesson plan. Condition: for one class of eight learners. Standard: times add to 90, outcomes are stated, and materials and safety notes are listed.

3.title: Teach a short lesson to a standard
3.intro: Now you teach. Show clearly, let learners try, and give kind, specific feedback.
pts: Show the skill slowly, then say what you did and why.
Break a skill into steps of one action each.
Check understanding by asking learners to show you, not just nod.
Give feedback on one thing at a time: what worked, what to try next.
3.ex: Instead of 'Good job', say: 'Your stitches are even. Next, try to keep your yarn tension the same on the return row.'
3.act: Teach a 20-minute mini lesson to three people and collect their feedback.
3.std: Task: teach a 20-minute lesson. Condition: to three volunteers. Standard: every learner completes the outcome and gives one useful comment.

4.title: Follow Canadian rules for classes and content
4.intro: Teaching to the public has rules about safety, advertising and other people's work.
pts: Advertising must be true. Do not promise results you cannot guarantee.
Copyright protects patterns, songs, books and images. Use your own material or material you have a licence for; check the current rule with the local authority.
Check the municipal rules for running classes at home or in a public space, including business licences and zoning.
Check whether your activity needs a certification or extra rules, such as food, fire, tools or children; check the current rule with the local authority.
4.ex: You want to hand out a pattern from a book. You make your own version instead, or ask the owner for written permission.
4.act: Make a table of rule, who sets it, what you must do and where you checked, for ten things in your class.
4.std: Task: build a class rules table. Condition: using official public pages. Standard: each row has a source and date; unclear items say 'check the current rule with the local authority'.

5.title: Cost and price a class
5.intro: You earn what is left after materials, space and time.
pts: Costs: materials per learner, space, tools, advertising, your prep and teaching time.
Price per learner = total costs plus your pay, divided by the number of learners, plus a small safety margin.
Know your break-even number of learners.
Sales tax may apply once you pass the small-supplier limit; check it with the tax agency.
5.ex: Costs: space 60, materials 8 per learner, your time 90. With 8 learners: cost = 60 + 64 + 90 = 214; price about 27 per learner. Teaching figures only.
5.act: Cost out a class and show the break-even number of learners.
5.std: Task: price one class. Condition: with a simple spreadsheet. Standard: costs, price and break-even are shown and a mentor can follow every number.

6.title: Find learners and promote honestly
6.intro: People join when they trust you and see what they will make.
pts: Describe the class in plain words: who it is for, what they will make, what to bring, how long.
Use photos of real work with permission.
Reach local groups, libraries and community boards with their permission.
Keep a list of enquiries and replies; send messages only to people who agreed to receive them.
6.ex: A poster says: 'Beginner watercolour, 2 hours, all materials included, 8 spaces. Make a small card to take home.'
6.act: Create a one-page class description and promote it to ten local places.
6.std: Task: promote one class. Condition: with permission and honest claims. Standard: the page states audience, outcome, time, price and what is included, and enquiries are logged.

7.title: Keep learners safe and protect your work
pts: Do a risk check: tools, heat, chemicals, allergies, floor space and first aid.
Ask learners about allergies and needs before class.
Write a short policy for cancellations, refunds and photos.
Protect learners' details and keep records of attendance.
7.ex: A woodcraft class lists: safety glasses worn, tools put away after use, first aid kit at the door.
7.act: Write a risk list and a one-page policy.
7.std: Task: produce a risk list and policy. Condition: reviewed by a mentor. Standard: each risk has a control and the policy covers refunds, photos and privacy.

8.title: Run a pilot course and decide
8.intro: Now you run a real course, measure and decide what to do next.
pts: Set a pilot goal: for example one four-week course with six learners.
Track attendance, cost, income and feedback each week.
Ask each learner what they made and what to improve.
Decide: stop, change or grow, and write a 12-month plan.
8.ex: After four weeks: 6 learners, 5 finished, 210 USD income, cost 120. You plan a second course with a waiting list.
8.act: Run the pilot and present your plan to a panel of three.
8.std: Task: run a four-week pilot. Condition: real learners and consent. Standard: log complete, outcomes met by most learners, decision uses numbers.

quiz: What is a learning outcome?
What a learner can do at the end of the class.
What shape does a good class have?
Welcome, show, try, feedback, try again, wrap-up.
Why have learners try during class?
People learn by doing, not only listening.
What makes feedback useful?
It is specific and about one thing at a time.
Why be careful with patterns, songs and images?
They are protected by copyright.
How do you find break-even?
Total costs divided by the price per learner.
What should a class page state?
Audience, outcome, time, price and what is included.
What do you ask learners before class?
About allergies and needs.
What do you do when unsure about a rule?
Check the current rule with the local authority.
What do you measure in a pilot?
Attendance, cost, income and feedback.
